claims.text: Fully homogenized equiatomic FeNiCrMn is a single-phase FCC alloy under the proposed initial conditions.
The dynamic mechanical behavior of equiatomic FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes is governed by transient Cr/Mn short-range-order clusters.
Transient Cr/Mn short-range-order clusters form within the FCC FeNiCrMn matrix.
Cr/Mn short-range-order clusters obstruct dislocation glide.
Reduced thermal activation at low temperature stabilizes Cr/Mn short-range-order clusters.
High strain rates stabilize Cr/Mn short-range-order clusters in FeNiCrMn.
Cluster stabilization at low temperature and high strain rate raises the yield strength of FeNiCrMn.
FeNiCrMn will exhibit increased strain-rate sensitivity at low temperatures and high strain rates.
The higher strength predicted at low temperature and high strain rate occurs at the expense of ductility.
At elevated temperatures or lower strain rates, thermal activation enables dislocations to bypass Cr/Mn short-range-order clusters or promotes cluster dissolution.
Reduced cluster effectiveness at elevated temperature or low strain rate lowers yield strength and improves ductility.
The proposed temperature-dependent cluster response maintains a favorable strength–ductility balance.
Low-temperature, high-rate FeNiCrMn specimens will have a higher density or stability of Cr/Mn short-range-order clusters.
Cluster density or stability will correlate with yield strength, ductility, and strain-rate sensitivity across the test regimes.
The short-range-order effect is minimal during quasi-static loading at 298 K.
Split-Hopkinson pressure-bar testing can impose compressive strain rates on the order of 10^3 s^-1, while conventional machines can impose quasi-static rates near 10^-3 s^-1.
Added phases or severe pre-existing defects may cause behavior outside the proposed single-phase FeNiCrMn mechanism.
Phonon drag may also contribute to increased yield stress at high strain rates.
Failure to find a significant correlation between cluster characteristics and mechanical performance would falsify the proposed mechanism.
